USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain current tariff posture but do not escalate further. Engage China in negotiations with the goal of reaching a deal before List 4A consumer tariffs hit Sept 1 and before the economy deteriorates further. The escalating cycle has reached a point where additional US tariffs will primarily hurt American consumers and businesses, while China has shown willingness to retaliate tit-for-tat.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading of +0.25 reflects that the trade war is producing real but not yet existential damage to US interests. On the negative side: US manufacturing PMI contracted to 49.9 in August (first time since 2009), new orders fell the most in a decade, export sales dropped to their lowest since 2009, GDP slowed from 3.1% to 2.1% in Q2, the yield curve inverted (a historically reliable recession predictor), and BBVA Research estimated 12-month recession probability above 40%. Consumer sentiment fell to its lowest since January with respondents citing tariff-driven price fears. These are concrete signs the trade war is biting the US economy directly.

However, the threat is not yet existential because: the services sector still shows expansion (50.9), farmers remain supportive of Trump (78% believe trade war will ultimately benefit agriculture per Purdue survey), the $28B farm subsidy cushion is in place, and the US retains significant leverage — China's economy is also slowing (GDP 6.2%, industrial production down to 4.8% in July) and faces structural challenges. The US labor market remains tight.

The action score of -0.15 (slight escalation lean, within negotiate band) reflects that the US should maintain pressure as a negotiating lever but should not add fuel to the fire. The Aug 23 escalation — where Trump ordered companies to find alternatives to China and raised List 4 to 15% after China's $75B retaliation — was rhetorically dramatic but practically dangerous. Further escalation risks: (1) List 4A hitting US consumers directly on Sept 1, just in time for back-to-school and early holiday purchasing; (2) China potentially weaponizing rare earths (90% of global supply; Xi visited a rare earth facility in May as a signal); (3) tipping the US manufacturing sector into full recession; (4) further yield curve inversion and market panic. The currency manipulator designation (Aug 5) was largely symbolic and may have hardened Beijing's stance rather than creating leverage.

The negotiate action is appropriate because: both sides have shown willingness to talk (G20 Osaka agreement, resumed talks in Shanghai), neither side has achieved a decisive advantage, and the economic costs of further escalation fall disproportionately on US consumers and farmers as tariffs expand to cover consumer goods. The political calendar also favors a deal — Trump needs a win before the 2020 election season intensifies, and farmers' patience is wearing thin (NYT Aug 27: 'growing number of farmers say they are losing patience'). Holding current tariff levels while pursuing negotiations preserves leverage without further damaging the domestic economy.
key_factors: US manufacturing PMI contracted to 49.9 — first contraction since Sept 2009
Yield curve inversion signals elevated recession risk (BBVA: >40% probability in 12 months)
GDP slowed from 3.1% to 2.1% in Q2; business expectations at lowest since 2012
List 4 tariffs (Sept 1) will directly hit US consumers for first time
China's rare earth leverage (90% of global supply) as potential retaliation card
Farmers showing early signs of patience wearing thin heading into 2020 election
China also under pressure (GDP 6.2%, IP 4.8%) — both sides face costs

sources_cited.excerpt: U.S. manufacturing PMI was 49.9 in August, below the neutral 50.0 threshold for the first time since September 2009. New orders dropped the most in 10 years, export sales tanked to lowest since August 2009.
Recession risk rises above 40% in next 12 months. GDP growth decelerated to 2.1% QoQa from 3.1%.
Trump announces 10% tariffs on remaining ~$300B of Chinese goods (List 4), effective Sept 1.
China announces retaliation on ~$75B of US goods. Trump orders US companies to find alternatives to China and raises List 4 rate to 15%.
China accounts for more than 90% of rare earths exports. NDRC statement prioritizing domestic supply was described as 'sound and valid.' Xi visited rare earth facility in May.
A growing number of farmers say they are losing patience with the president's approach and are suggesting it will not take much to lose their vote.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Retaliate proportionally to the latest US escalation while preserving room for negotiation. Maintain the $75B retaliatory tariffs announced Aug 23 and prepare measured counter-measures (unreliable entity list, rare earth export controls) as leverage, but avoid actions that would close the door to talks entirely. The domestic economy needs stability more than a maximalist standoff.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is severe but not yet existential. On the damage side: List 3 tariffs at 25% cover $250B of Chinese exports, with List 4A (Sept 1) and 4B (Dec 15) adding ~$300B more at 10-15% — meaning nearly all Chinese exports to the US face tariffs (timeline: Aug 1, Aug 13, Aug 23). Huawei and affiliates remain on the Entity List since May 16, cutting off critical US semiconductor and software supply chains. GDP slowed to 6.2% in Q2, a 27-year low (Reuters, Jul 15). Exports to the US fell 8.1% in H1 (CNN, Jul 15). Factories are shedding jobs at the fastest pace since the 2008 crisis (Reuters, Jul 15). The yuan has broken past 7 to an 11-year low (CNBC, Aug 28), and the US Treasury designated China a currency manipulator on Aug 5 — a new vector of pressure. FX reserves fell $15.5B in July to $3.1T (Reuters, Aug 13). Trump's Aug 23 'order' for US companies to leave China, while legally dubious (Vox, Aug 24; Paul Weiss analysis, Aug 26), signals an intent to pursue economic decoupling beyond tariffs.

However, several factors prevent this from reading as existential: (1) China's growth at 6.2% is still within the 6-6.5% target range, and Beijing has fiscal stimulus room — 2T yuan tax cuts and 2.15T yuan local government bond quota already deployed (Reuters, Jul 15). (2) June industrial production rebounded to 6.3% and retail sales jumped 9.8% (CNBC, Jul 15), suggesting stimulus is starting to bite. (3) The weak yuan, while triggering the manipulator label, partially offsets tariff costs for exporters. (4) China has asymmetric leverage: $3.1T in reserves, rare earth supply dominance (Xi's May 20 Jiangxi visit was a deliberate signal), the unreliable entity list announced May 31, and the ability to target US agricultural imports in farm-belt states ahead of the 2020 election. (5) Trump's company 'order' lacks legal authority and was walked back at the G7 — the US side is also under pressure, with the Dow dropping 623 points on Aug 23 and recession fears rising.

The action stance of retaliation at -0.3 reflects a measured response. China already retaliated on Aug 23 with $75B in tariffs. Further immediate escalation risks a spiral that China's slowing economy cannot afford, but conceding now — after Trump raised List 4 to 15% the same day — would signal weakness and invite further pressure. The right posture is to hold retaliatory measures in place, signal willingness to resume talks (trade talks were still nominally ongoing per Peter Navarro's Aug 23 statement), and use the remaining leverage (rare earths, entity list, agricultural purchases) as bargaining chips rather than deploying them now.
key_factors: List 4 tariffs at 10-15% covering ~$300B of remaining Chinese exports effective Sept 1 / Dec 15
Huawei entity list cutting off US semiconductor supply chains since May 16
Q2 GDP at 6.2% — 27-year low, within target but signaling real deceleration
Yuan past 7 to 11-year low; US currency manipulator designation Aug 5
Trump's Aug 23 'order' for US companies to leave China signals decoupling intent
China's asymmetric leverage: rare earths, $3.1T reserves, agricultural import targeting
Dow -623 on Aug 23; US recession fears constrain Trump's escalation appetite
Trade talks nominally continuing (Navarro statement Aug 23)

sources_cited.excerpt: China announces retaliation on ~$75B of US goods (5-10%, split Sept 1 / Dec 15), including re-imposing tariffs on US autos. Trump orders US companies to 'immediately start looking for an alternative to China' and directs a 5-point increase on the planned List 4 rate (to 15%) and threatened hikes on existing lists.
After the Shanghai round, Trump announces 10% tariffs on the remaining ~$300B of Chinese goods (List 4), effective Sept 1.
After CNY breaks 7 per USD, US Treasury designates China a currency manipulator (first such designation since 1994).
US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.
China's economic growth slowed to 6.2% in the second quarter, its weakest pace in at least 27 years, as demand at home and abroad faltered in the face of mounting U.S. trade pressure.
The onshore yuan fell to levels not seen since February 2008 on Monday, and the offshore yuan dropped to its weakest since it began trading in the international market around 2010.
China's foreign exchange reserves - the world's largest - fall by $15.54 billion in July to $3.104 trillion, central bank data showed, amid rising trade tensions.
